statement_tex:
\label{thm:sos_technical}

Let $k\geq 1$ be an integer and let $\eps > 0$. Let $\AELC$ be a
code obtained using the AEL construction using  $(G, \calC_{\out}, \calC_{\inn})$, where $\calC_{\inn}$ is $(\delta_0, k, \eps/2)$ average-radius list decodable with erasures, and $G$ is a $(n,d,\lambda)$-expander. 

Suppose that $\calC_{\out}$ is unique decodable from radius $\delta_{\out}^{\dec}$ in time $\calT(n)$.

If $\lambda \leq \frac{\delta_{\out}^{\dec}}{12{k}^{k}} \cdot \eps$, then there is a deterministic algorithm that takes as input $g\in (\Sigma_{\inn}^d)^R$, runs in time $\calT(n) + n^{O\inparen{ \frac{d \cdot k^{3k}|\Sigma_{\inn}|^{3kd}}{(\delta_{\out}^{\dec})^2\cdot \eps^2}}}$, and outputs the list $\calL(g,\frac{k-1}{k}(\delta_0-\eps))$.

Suppose that C _ out is unique decodable from radius δ_ out ^ dec in time T (n) . label: cor:algo-main
paper_title: Explicit Codes approaching Generalized Singleton Bound using Expanders
statement_tex:
\label{cor:algo-main}
For every $\rho, \eps \in (0,1)$ and $k \in \N$, there exist explicit inner codes $\calC_{\inn}$ and an infinite family explicit codes $\AELC \subseteq (\F_q^d)^n$ obtained via the AEL construction that satisfy: 
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\rho(\AELC) \geq \rho$
\item For any $g \in  (\F_q^d)^n$ and any $\calH \subseteq \AELC$ with $\abs{\calH} \leq k$ that
\[
\sum_{h \in \calH} \Delta(g,h) ~\geq~ (\abs{\calH}-1) \cdot (1 - \rho - \eps) \mper
\]
\item The alphabet size $q^d$ of the code $\AELC$ can be taken to be $2^{O(k^{3k}/\eps^9)}$.
\item $\AELC$ can be decoded from radius $\frac{k-1}{k}(1-\rho-\eps)$ in time $n^{2^{O(k^{4k}/\eps^{10})}}$ with a list of size at most $k-1$.
\end{enumerate}
statement_text: For every ρ, ε ∈ (0,1) and k ∈ N , there exist explicit inner codes C _ in and an infinite family explicit codes C _ AEL ⊆ ( F _q^d)^n obtained via the AEL construction that satisfy: ρ( C _ AEL ) ≥ ρ For any g ∈ ( F _q^d)^n and any H ⊆ C _ AEL with abs H ≤ k that \[ Σ _ h ∈ H Δ(g,h) ≥ (abs H -1) · (1 - ρ - ε) . \] The alphabet size q^d of the code C _ AEL can be taken to be 2^ O(k^ 3k /ε^9) . C _ AEL can be decoded from radius frac k-1 k (1-ρ-ε) in time n^ 2^ O(k^ 4k /ε^ 10 ) with a list of size at most k-1 .

paper_title: PCP-free APX-Hardness of Nearest Codeword and Minimum Distance
statement_text: Fix any finite field F_q . Given n variables x_1, ... ,x_n and m quadratic equations Q_1(xx^T)=0, ... , Q_m(xx^T)=0 , it is NP-hard to distinguish between the following two cases: sep=0ex (YES) There exists a non-zero vector x ∈ {0,1}^n satisfying all m equations. (NO) There is no non-zero x ∈ F_q^n satisfying all m equations. Furthermore, the hardness holds with the distinguished-coordinate property, i.e., in the YES case, there is a non-zero vector x satisfying all equations as well as x_n=1 .
title: Homogeneous Quadratic Equations Hardness

statement_tex:
Suppose $f\in\mathscr{M}_P$ is of arity $k$ and $(S_1,S_2)$ is a partition of $\{1,2,\dots,k\}$. Let $ST_f$ be the star gadget that realize $f$ as described in Lemma \ref{lem:SymGadRealize} and $h_f$ be the symmetric central signature. For $q=|S_1|$, let $PP_q=(V,E,D)=uxwyv$ be the $q$-path gadget of $h_f$, and we replace $h_f$ with the $PP_q$ gadget in $ST_f$ to obtain the gadget $ST_f'$, such that variables with indices in $S_1$ are connecting to the head of $PP_q$, while those corresponding to $S_2$ are connecting to the tail.
    
    A $(S_1,S_2)$-path gadget $PP_{(S_1,S_2)}=(V,E,D)$ of $f$ is defined as follows. The underlying graph of $PP_{(S_1,S_2)}$ is same as $PP_q$. $x,w,y$ are assigned the same signature as in $ST_f'$. $u$ is assigned the signature of the gadget formed by the $q$ edge signatures with indices in $S_1$ and the signature assigned to the head vertex of $PP_q$ in $ST_f'$. In other words, it is the signature of the gadget induced by $\{u\}\cup N_u-x$ in the gadget $ST_f'$, where $N_u$ denotes the neighbours of $u$ in $ST_F'$ and each vertex in $N_u-x$ is assigned the edge signature with index belonging to $S_1$. The signature assigned to $v$ is analogous to that assigned to $u$, except that it is of arity $k-q+1$ and the indices of its variables correspond to $S_2$.

    We denote $u$ as the head vertex of $PP_{(S_1,S_2)}$ and $v$ as the tail vertex of $PP_{(S_1,S_2)}$ in this case as well.
    \label{defpath}

label: def:span-program
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{def:span-program}
        A span program consists of the following mathematical objects:
        \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
            \item The \textit{state space}: A Hilbert space $\H$ of finite dimension.
            \item The \textit{domain}: A finite set $\D$, whose elements are referred to as \textit{inputs}.
            \item The \textit{input-dependent subspaces}: to every input $x \in \D$, we associate an input-dependent subspace $\H(x) \subseteq \H$.
            \item The \textit{input-independent subspace}: A subspace $\K \subseteq \H$.
            \item The \textit{initial vector}: $0 \neq \ket{w_0} \in \K^{\perp}$.
        \end{enumerate}
        Then, $\mathcal{P} = (\H, x \mapsto \H(x), \K, \ket{w_0})$ is a span program on $\D$. We make a distinction between positive and negative inputs, as such:
        \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
            \item $x \in \D$ is a \textit{positive input}, if $\ket{w_0} \in \K + \H(x)$.
            \item $x \in \D$ is a \textit{negative input}, if $\ket{w_0} \not\in \K + \H(x)$.
        \end{enumerate}
        Finally, we let $f : \D \to \{0,1\}$ be the function that evaluates to $1$ if and only if the input $x \in \D$ is positive. We say that $\mathcal{P}$ computes $f$.

The it domain : A finite set D , whose elements are referred to as it inputs . The it input-dependent subspaces : to every input x ∈ D , we associate an input-dependent subspace H (x) ⊆ H . The it input-independent subspace : A subspace K ⊆ H . The it initial vector : 0 ≠ |w_0 rangle ∈ K ^ perp . Then, P = ( H , x mapsto H (x), K , |w_0 rangle ) is a span program on D . We make a distinction between positive and negative inputs, as such: x ∈ D is a it positive input , if |w_0 rangle ∈ K + H (x) . x ∈ D is a it negative input , if |w_0 rangle ∉ K + H (x) . Finally, we let f : D → {0,1} be the function that evaluates to 1 if and only if the input x ∈ D is positive. We say that P computes f .
title: Span programs

label: def:witnesses
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{def:witnesses}
        Let $\mathcal{P} = (\H, x \mapsto \H(x), \K, \ket{w_0})$ be a span program on $\D$ that computes $f$. Then,
        \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
            \item If $x \in \D$ is a positive input, then every vector $\ket{w_x} \in \H(x)$ that satisfies $\ket{w_x} - \ket{w_0} \in \K$ is a positive witness for $x$. We write $\W_+(x,\mathcal{P})$ for the set of these vectors. The positive witness complexity for $x$ is the minimal norm-squared of such vectors, and it's denoted by $w_+(x,\mathcal{P})$, which is $\infty$ if such a vector does not exist.
            \item If $x \in \D$ is a negative input, then every vector $\ket{w_x} \in \K^{\perp} \cap \H(x)^{\perp}$ for which $\braket{w_x}{w_0} = 1$ is a negative witness for $x$. We write $\W_-(x,\mathcal{P})$ for the set of these vectors. The negative witness complexity for $x$ is the minimal norm-squared of such vectors, and it's denoted by $w_-(x,\mathcal{P})$, which is $\infty$ if such a vector does not exist.
            \item We define the positive and negative witness complexity, $W_+(\mathcal{P})$ and $W_-(\mathcal{P})$, respectively, as
            \[W_+(\mathcal{P}) = \max_{x \in f^{-1}(1)} w_+(x,\mathcal{P}), \qquad \text{and} \qquad W_-(\mathcal{P}) = \max_{x \in f^{-1}(0)} w_-(x,\mathcal{P}),\]
            and we define the span program complexity, $C(\mathcal{P})$, as
            \[C(\mathcal{P}) = \sqrt{W_+(\mathcal{P}) \cdot W_-(\mathcal{P})}.\]
        \end{enumerate}
statement_text: Let P = ( H , x mapsto H (x), K , |w_0 rangle ) be a span program on D that computes f . Then, If x ∈ D is a positive input, then every vector |w_x rangle ∈ H (x) that satisfies |w_x rangle - |w_0 rangle ∈ K is a positive witness for x . We write W _+(x, P ) for the set of these vectors. The positive witness complexity for x is the minimal norm-squared of such vectors, and it's denoted by w_+(x, P ) , which is ∞ if such a vector does not exist. If x ∈ D is a negative input, then every vector |w_x rangle ∈ K ^ perp ∩ H (x)^ perp for which lew_xmiddle |w_0 rangle = 1 is a negative witness for x . We write W _-(x, P ) for the set of these vectors. The negative witness complexity for x is the minimal norm-squared of such vectors, and it's denoted by w_-(x, P ) , which is ∞ if such a vector does not exist. We define the positive and negative witness complexity, W_+( P ) and W_-( P ) , respectively, as \[W_+( P ) = max _ x ∈ f^ -1 (1) w_+(x, P ), qquad and qquad W_-( P ) = max _ x ∈ f^ -1 (0) w_-(x, P ),\] and we define the span program complexity, C( P ) , as \[C( P ) = sqrt W_+( P ) · W_-( P ) .\]
title: Span program witnesses

statement_tex:
Let $\mathcal{P}$ be a span program on $\D$, and $\alpha > 0$. Then, for all $x \in \D$
        \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
            \item $\W_+(x,\alpha\mathcal{P}) = \W_+(x,\mathcal{P}) \cdot \alpha$, and so $w_+(x,\alpha\mathcal{P}) = w_+(x,\mathcal{P}) \cdot \alpha$.
            \item $\W_-(x,\alpha\mathcal{P}) = \W_-(x,\mathcal{P})/\alpha$, and so $w_-(x,\alpha\mathcal{P}) = w_-(x,\mathcal{P})/\alpha$.
            \item $W_+(\alpha\mathcal{P}) = \alpha W_+(\mathcal{P})$, $W_-(\alpha\mathcal{P}) = W_-(\mathcal{P})/\alpha$, and so $C(\alpha\mathcal{P}) = C(\mathcal{P})$.
            \item If $\mathcal{P}$ computes $f$, then so does $\alpha\mathcal{P}$.
        \end{enumerate}
statement_text: Let P be a span program on D , and α > 0 . Then, for all x ∈ D W _+(x,α P ) = W _+(x, P ) · α , and so w_+(x,α P ) = w_+(x, P ) · α . W _-(x,α P ) = W _-(x, P )/α , and so w_-(x,α P ) = w_-(x, P )/α . W_+(α P ) = α W_+( P ) , W_-(α P ) = W_-( P )/α , and so C(α P ) = C( P ) . If P computes f , then so does α P .
title: Properties of scalar multiplication of span programs

statement_tex:
Let $\mathcal{P} = (\H, x \mapsto \H(x), \K, \ket{w_0})$ be a span program on $\D$. We define:
        \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
            \item For all $x \in \D$, $\H'(x) = \H(x)^{\perp}$,
            \item $\K' = (\K \oplus \Span\{\ket{w_0}\})^{\perp}$,
            \item $\ket{w_0'} = \ket{w_0}/\norm{\ket{w_0}}^2$.
        \end{enumerate}
        Then $\lnot\mathcal{P} = (\H, x \mapsto \H'(x), \K', \ket{w_0'})$ is the negation of $\mathcal{P}$.

label: thm:negation
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{thm:negation}
        Let $\mathcal{P}$ be a span program on $\D$.
        \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
            \item For all $x \in \D$, $\mathcal{W}_-(x,\lnot\mathcal{P}) = \mathcal{W}_+(x,\mathcal{P})$, and so $w_-(x,\lnot\mathcal{P}) = w_+(x,\mathcal{P})$.
            \item For all $x \in \D$, $\mathcal{W}_+(x,\lnot\mathcal{P}) = \mathcal{W}_-(x,\mathcal{P})$, and so $w_+(x,\lnot\mathcal{P}) = w_-(x,\mathcal{P})$.
            \item $W_-(\lnot\mathcal{P}) = W_+(\mathcal{P})$, $W_+(\lnot\mathcal{P}) = W_-(\mathcal{P})$, and $C(\lnot\mathcal{P}) = C(\mathcal{P})$.
            \item If $\mathcal{P}$ computes $f$, then $\lnot\mathcal{P}$ computes $\lnot f$.
        \end{enumerate}
statement_text: Let P be a span program on D . For all x ∈ D , W _-(x, ¬ P ) = W _+(x, P ) , and so w_-(x, ¬ P ) = w_+(x, P ) . For all x ∈ D , W _+(x, ¬ P ) = W _-(x, P ) , and so w_+(x, ¬ P ) = w_-(x, P ) . W_-( ¬ P ) = W_+( P ) , W_+( ¬ P ) = W_-( P ) , and C( ¬ P ) = C( P ) . If P computes f , then ¬ P computes ¬ f .
title: Properties of span program negation

label: thm:feasible-sln-adv-bound
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{thm:feasible-sln-adv-bound}
        Let $\mathcal{P} = (\H, x \mapsto \H(x), \K, \ket{w_0})$ be a span program on $\D$, computing the function $f : \D \to \{0,1\}$. For all $x \in \D$, let $\ket{w_x}$ be a span program witness, i.e., if $f(x) = 0$, let $\ket{w_x} \in \W_-(x,\mathcal{P})$, and if $f(x) = 1$, let $\ket{w_x} \in \W_+(x,\mathcal{P})$, cf.\ \cref{def:witnesses}. label: def:electrical-networks
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{def:electrical-networks}
        Let $G = (V,E)$ be an undirected graph, with \textit{resistances} $r : E \to [0,\infty]$. With every edge $e \in E$, we associate a default direction, i.e., it has a head $e_+$ and a tail $e_-$. We also write $N_+(v), N_-(v) \subseteq E$ to be the set of outgoing and incoming edges to $V$, respectively. Now, we define the following objects:
        \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
            \item The Hilbert space $\H_G = \C^E$ is the \textit{flow space} of $G$, i.e., the set $\{\ket{e} : e \in E\}$ forms an orthonormal basis of the complex Hilbert space $\H_G$.
            \item Every function $f : E \to \C$ that satisfies $f_e = 0$ if $r_e = \infty$ is a \textit{flow} on $G$. To every flow $f$ on $G$, we associate a \textit{flow state} $\ket{f_{G,r}} = \sum_{e \in E} f_e\sqrt{r_e}\ket{e} \in \H_G$, where here and in the following we take $0 \cdot \infty = 0$. Sometimes, we write $\ket{f}$ instead of $\ket{f_{G,r}}$, if the graph and the resistances are clear from context.
            \item If a flow $f$ on $G$ satisfies for all $v \in V$, $\sum_{e \in N_+(v)} f_e - \sum_{e \in N_-(v)} f_e = 0$, then $f$ is a \textit{circulation}. We denote the set of circulations by $C_G$, and the \textit{circulation space} is $\mathcal{C}_{G,r} = \{\ket{f_{G,r}} : f \in C_G\} \subseteq \H_G$.
            \item Let $s,t \in V$ with $s \neq t$. If a flow $f$ on $G$ satisfies
            \[\sum_{e \in N_+(v)} f_e - \sum_{e \in N_-(v)} f_e = \begin{cases}
                1, & \text{if } v = s, \\
                -1, & \text{if } v = t, \\
                0, & \text{otherwise},
            \end{cases}\]
            then $f$ is a \textit{unit $st$-flow} on $G$. We let $ F_{G,s,t}$ be the set of all unit $st$-flows on $G$, and the \textit{unit-$st$-flow space} on $G$ is $\mathcal{F}_{G,s,t,r} = \{\ket{f_{G,r}} : f \in F_{G,s,t}\} \subseteq \H_G$. We say that $s$ and $t$ are \textit{connected} in $G$ if $F_{G,s,t}$ is non-empty.
            \item Let $f$ be a flow on $G$. The norm squared of $\ket{f}$, i.e., $\norm{\ket{f_{G,r}}}^2 = \sum_{e \in E} |f_e|^2r_e$ is the \textit{energy} of $f$. If $s$ and $t$ are connected in $G$, we define the \textit{minimum-energy unit $st$-flow} and the \textit{effective resistance} between $s$ and $t$, respectively, by
            \[f^{\min}_{G,s,t,r} := \underset{f \in F_{G,s,t}}\argmin \norm{\ket{f_{G,r}}}^2, \qquad \text{and} \qquad R_{G,s,t,r} := \norm{\ket{f^{\min}_{G,s,t,r}}}^2.\]
            On the other hand, if $s$ and $t$ are not connected in $G$, then $R_{G,s,t,r} = \infty$.
        \end{enumerate}

We also write N_+(v), N_-(v) ⊆ E to be the set of outgoing and incoming edges to V , respectively. Now, we define the following objects: The Hilbert space H _G = C ^E is the it flow space of G , i.e., the set { |e rangle : e ∈ E} forms an orthonormal basis of the complex Hilbert space H _G . Every function f : E → C that satisfies f_e = 0 if r_e = ∞ is a it flow on G . To every flow f on G , we associate a it flow state |f_ G,r rangle = Σ _ e ∈ E f_e sqrt r_e |e rangle ∈ H _G , where here and in the following we take 0 · ∞ = 0 . Sometimes, we write |f rangle instead of |f_ G,r rangle , if the graph and the resistances are clear from context. If a flow f on G satisfies for all v ∈ V , Σ _ e ∈ N_+(v) f_e - Σ _ e ∈ N_-(v) f_e = 0 , then f is a it circulation . We denote the set of circulations by C_G , and the it circulation space is C _ G,r = { |f_ G,r rangle : f ∈ C_G} ⊆ H _G . Let s,t ∈ V with s ≠ t . If a flow f on G satisfies \[ Σ _ e ∈ N_+(v) f_e - Σ _ e ∈ N_-(v) f_e = 1, & if v = s, -1, & if v = t, 0, & otherwise , \] then f is a it unit st -flow on G . We let F_ G,s,t be the set of all unit st -flows on G , and the it unit- st -flow space on G is F _ G,s,t,r = { |f_ G,r rangle : f ∈ F_ G,s,t } ⊆ H _G . We say that s and t are it connected in G if F_ G,s,t is non-empty. Let f be a flow on G . The norm squared of |f rangle , i.e., | |f_ G,r rangle | ^2 = Σ _ e ∈ E |f_e|^2r_e is the it energy of f . If s and t are connected in G , we define the it minimum-energy unit st -flow and the it effective resistance between s and t , respectively, by \[f^ min _ G,s,t,r := underset f ∈ F_ G,s,t argmin | |f_ G,r rangle | ^2, qquad and qquad R_ G,s,t,r := | |f^ min _ G,s,t,r rangle | ^2.\] On the other hand, if s and t are not connected in G , then R_ G,s,t,r = ∞ .

statement_tex:
Let $G = (V,E)$ be an undirected graph with resistances $r : E \to [0,\infty]$. A \textit{potential function} on $G$ is a function $U : V \to \C$, such that for all $e \in E$ where $r_e = 0$, we have $U_{e_-} = U_{e_+}$. We define a flow $f_{G,U,r}$ derived from the potential $U$, such that for all $e \in E$,
        \[(f_{G,U,r})_e := \frac{U_{e_-} - U_{e_+}}{r_e},\]
        where we use the convention that $0/0 = 0$. We refer to $\ket{f_{G,U,r}}$ as the \textit{potential state}.

label: thm:potential-function-properties
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{thm:potential-function-properties}
        Let $G = (V,E)$ be an undirected graph with resistances $r : E \to [0,\infty]$. We have the following properties of potential functions:
        \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
            \item A flow state is a potential state if and only if it is orthogonal to the circulation subspace.
            \item For any potential function $U$ on $G$ and any unit $st$-flow $f$ on $G$, we have $\braket{f_{G,r}}{f_{G,U,r}} = U_s - U_t$.
            \item We have
            \[\min_{\substack{U \text{ potential on } G \\ U_s - U_t = 1}} \norm{\ket{f_{G,U,r}}}^2 = R^{-1}_{G,s,t,r}.\]
        \end{enumerate}

We have the following properties of potential functions: A flow state is a potential state if and only if it is orthogonal to the circulation subspace. We have \[min _ substack U potential on G U_s - U_t = 1 | |f_ G,U,r rangle | ^2 = R^ -1 _ G,s,t,r .\]

statement_tex:
\label{def:graph-composition}
        Let $G = (V,E)$ be a connected, undirected graph. Let $\D$ be a finite set, and for every edge $e \in E$, let $\mathcal{P}^e = (\H^e, x \mapsto \H^e(x), \K^e, \ket{w_0^e})$ be a span program on $\D$. Let $s,t \in V$ with $s \neq t$, such that $s$ and $t$ are connected in $G$. For all $e \in E$, we write $r_e = \norm{\ket{w_0^e}}^2$. For all $x \in \D$, we let
        \[\H = \bigoplus_{e \in E} \H^e, \qquad \text{and} \qquad \H(x) = \bigoplus_{e \in E} \H^e(x).\]
        Now, we define $\mathcal{E} : \H_G \to \H$ as a linear isometric embedding that for all $e \in E$ maps $\ket{e} \mapsto \ket{w_0^e}/\norm{\ket{w_0^e}}$. We let
        \[\K = \bigoplus_{e \in E} \K^e \oplus \mathcal{E}(\mathcal{C}_{G,r}), \qquad \text{and} \qquad \ket{w_0} = \mathcal{E}\left(\ket{f^{\min}_{G,s,t,r}}\right).\]
        The span program $\mathcal{P} = (\H, x \mapsto \H(x), \K, \ket{w_0})$ is the graph composition of $G$ with source node $s$, sink node $t$, and span programs $(\mathcal{P}^e)_{e \in E}$.

Let s,t ∈ V with s ≠ t , such that s and t are connected in G . For all e ∈ E , we write r_e = | |w_0^e rangle | ^2 . For all x ∈ D , we let \[ H = oplus_ e ∈ E H ^e, qquad and qquad H (x) = oplus_ e ∈ E H ^e(x).\] Now, we define E : H _G → H as a linear isometric embedding that for all e ∈ E maps |e rangle mapsto |w_0^e rangle / | |w_0^e rangle | . We let \[ K = oplus_ e ∈ E K ^e ⊕ E ( C _ G,r ), qquad and qquad |w_0 rangle = E ( |f^ min _ G,s,t,r rangle ).\] The span program P = ( H , x mapsto H (x), K , |w_0 rangle ) is the graph composition of G with source node s , sink node t , and span programs ( P ^e)_ e ∈ E .

statement_text: Let G = (V,E) be an undirected graph, and let s,t ∈ V with s ≠ t , such that s and t are connected in G . label: thm:spectral-method
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{thm:spectral-method}
        Let $G = (V,E)$ be an undirected graph with resistances $r : E \to \R_{>0}$. For all $v \in V$, let $N(v) \subseteq E$ be the set of edges incident to $v$. Let
        \[U_{G,r} : \ket{v}\ket{\bot} \mapsto \ket{v} \left[\sum_{e \in N(v)} \frac{1}{r_e}\right]^{-\frac12}\sum_{e \in N(v)} \frac{1}{\sqrt{r_e}}\ket{e}.\]
        Then, we can implement the reflection through $\mathcal{C}_{G,r}$ with $\widetilde{O}(1/\sqrt{\delta})$ call to $U_{G,r}$ and $\widetilde{O}(1/\sqrt{\delta})$ additional gates, where $\delta$ is the smallest non-zero eigenvalue of the symmetrically normalized Laplacian of $G$, which is defined as $L \in \R^{V \times V}$, with
        \[L[v,w] = \frac{\sum_{e \in N(v) \cap N(w)} \frac{1}{r_e}}{\sqrt{\sum_{e \in N(v)} \frac{1}{r_e} \cdot \sum_{e \in N(w)} \frac{1}{r_e}}}.\]
statement_text: Let G = (V,E) be an undirected graph with resistances r : E → R _ >0 . For all v ∈ V , let N(v) ⊆ E be the set of edges incident to v . Let \[U_ G,r : |v rangle |bot rangle mapsto |v rangle [ Σ _ e ∈ N(v) frac 1 r_e ]^ -frac 12 Σ _ e ∈ N(v) frac 1 sqrt r_e |e rangle .\] Then, we can implement the reflection through C _ G,r with widetilde O (1/ sqrt δ ) call to U_ G,r and widetilde O (1/ sqrt δ ) additional gates, where δ is the smallest non-zero eigenvalue of the symmetrically normalized Laplacian of G , which is defined as L ∈ R ^ V × V , with \[L[v,w] = frac Σ _ e ∈ N(v) ∩ N(w) frac 1 r_e sqrt Σ _ e ∈ N(v) frac 1 r_e · Σ _ e ∈ N(w) frac 1 r_e .\]

label: def:tree-parallel-decomposition
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{def:tree-parallel-decomposition}
        Let $G = (V,E)$ be an undirected graph with resistances $r : E \to \R_{>0}$. Let $E_1, \dots, E_k$ be a partition of $E$ such that each of the $E_j$'s is not empty, and for all $j \in [k]$, let $V_j = \{v \in V : N(v) \cap E_j \neq \varnothing\}$.
        \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
            \item \textit{Tree decomposition.} Suppose that for all $j,j' \in [k]$ with $j \neq j'$, we have $|V_j \cap V_{j'}| \leq 1$. Let $G' = (V',E')$ be the graph where we contract all of the edge sets $E_1, \dots, E_k$ into a single edge and then prune the edges that have a loose end, i.e., formally we write $V' = \{v_{j,j'} : \{j,j'\} \subseteq [k]^2 \land j \neq j' \land V_j \cap V_{j'} = \{v_{j,j'}\}\}$ and $E' = \{\{v_{j,j'},v_{\ell,\ell'}\} \in (V')^2 : |\{j,j',\ell,\ell'\}| = 3 \land v_{j,j'} \neq v_{\ell,\ell'}\}$ as a multiset. Suppose that $G'$ is a tree. Then, we refer to $G|_{E_1}, \dots, G|_{E_k}$ as a \textit{tree decomposition} of $G$.
            \item \textit{Parallel decomposition.} If there exist $s,t \in V$ with $s \neq t$, such that for all $j,j' \in [k]$ with $j \neq j'$, $V_j \cap V_{j'} = \{s,t\}$, then we refer to $G|_{E_1}, \dots, G|_{E_k}$ as a \textit{parallel decomposition} of $G$.
        \end{enumerate}
        Finally, let $T$ be a tree, where every node is labeled by a subset of $E$, such that:
        \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
            \item The root node is labeled by $E$.
            \item Every leaf is labeled by a single edge $\{e\}$, with $e \in E$.
            \item If an internal node is labeled by $E'$ and all its children are labeled by $E_1, \dots, E_k$, then $G|_{E_1}, \dots, G|_{E_k}$ is a tree or parallel decomposition of $G|_{E'}$.
        \end{enumerate}
        Then, we refer to $T$ as a \textit{tree-parallel decomposition} of $G$.
statement_text: Let G = (V,E) be an undirected graph with resistances r : E → R _ >0 . Let E_1, ... , E_k be a partition of E such that each of the E_j 's is not empty, and for all j ∈ [k] , let V_j = {v ∈ V : N(v) ∩ E_j ≠ varnothing } . it Tree decomposition. Suppose that for all j,j' ∈ [k] with j ≠ j' , we have |V_j ∩ V_ j' | ≤ 1 . Let G' = (V',E') be the graph where we contract all of the edge sets E_1, ... , E_k into a single edge and then prune the edges that have a loose end, i.e., formally we write V' = {v_ j,j' : {j,j'} ⊆ [k]^2 ∧ j ≠ j' ∧ V_j ∩ V_ j' = {v_ j,j' }} and E' = {{v_ j,j' ,v_ ell ,ell ' } ∈ (V')^2 : |{j,j',ell ,ell '}| = 3 ∧ v_ j,j' ≠ v_ ell ,ell ' } as a multiset. Suppose that G' is a tree. Then, we refer to G|_ E_1 , ... , G|_ E_k as a it tree decomposition of G . it Parallel decomposition. If there exist s,t ∈ V with s ≠ t , such that for all j,j' ∈ [k] with j ≠ j' , V_j ∩ V_ j' = {s,t} , then we refer to G|_ E_1 , ... , G|_ E_k as a it parallel decomposition of G . Finally, let T be a tree, where every node is labeled by a subset of E , such that: The root node is labeled by E . Every leaf is labeled by a single edge {e} , with e ∈ E . If an internal node is labeled by E' and all its children are labeled by E_1, ... , E_k , then G|_ E_1 , ... , G|_ E_k is a tree or parallel decomposition of G|_ E' . Then, we refer to T as a it tree-parallel decomposition of G .

label: thm:implementation-circuit-model
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{thm:implementation-circuit-model}
        Let $G = (V,E)$ be a graph with resistances $r : E \to \R_{>0}$, and let $T$ be a tree-parallel decomposition of the circulation space of $G$, with depth $d$. For every $\ell \in [d]$, let $k_{\ell}$ be the maximum number of children of nodes in the $(\ell-1)$th vertex layer. We use a Hilbert space $\C^{[k_1] \cup \{\bot\}} \otimes \cdots \otimes \C^{[k_d] \cup \{\bot\}}$, with dimension $K = (k_1+1) \cdots (k_d+1)$.

        Every node $u$ in $T$ is connected to its root by a unique path. If $u$ is in the $\ell$th vertex layer, we write $u = (j_1, \dots, j_\ell)$, if $u$ is reached through starting at the root node and taking the $j_{\ell'}$th child at the $(\ell'-1)$th vertex layer, for all $\ell' \in [\ell]$. Moreover, since every leaf $u = (j_1, \dots, j_d)$ is uniquely labeled by a singleton $\{e\}$, we identify
        \[\ket{e} := \ket{j_1, \dots, j_d}.\]

        Next, let an internal node $u \in V$ be labeled by $E_u$, and let $u_1, \dots, u_k$ be its children, labeled by $E_{u_1}, \dots, E_{u_k}$. Suppose that $G|_{E_{u_1}}, \dots, G|_{E_{u_k}}$ is a parallel decomposition of $G|_{E_u}$, with source and sink nodes $s$ and $t$. For all $j \in [k]$, we write
        \[\ket{\psi_u} := \sum_{j=1}^k \frac{1}{\norm{\ket{f_{u,j}}}}\ket{j}, \qquad \text{with} \qquad \ket{f_{u,j}} := \ket{f^{\min}_{G|_{E_{u_j}}, s, t, r|_{E_{u_j}}}}.\]

        Now, for every $\ell \in [d]$, we write the operation $\mathcal{E}_{\ell}$ that for all $u = (j_1, \dots, j_{\ell-1})$ in the $(\ell-1)$th layer of $T$ acts for all $j \in [k]$,
        \[\mathcal{E}_{\ell} : \ket{j_1,\dots,j_{\ell-1}}\ket{j}\ket{\bot}^{\otimes(d-\ell)} \mapsto \begin{cases}
            \ket{j_1,\dots,j_{\ell-1}}\ket{j}\ket{\bot}^{\otimes(d-\ell)}, & \text{if } u \text{ is the root of a tree decomposition}, \\
            \ket{j_1,\dots,j_{\ell-1}}\ket{j}\frac{\ket{f_{u,j}}}{\norm{\ket{f_{u,j}}}}, & \text{otherwise}.
        \end{cases}\]

        Similarly, for all $\ell \in [d]$, we write $U_{\ell}$ as the operation that for all $u = (j_1, \dots, j_{\ell-1})$ in the $(\ell-1)$th layer of $T$ acts as
        \[U_{\ell} : \ket{j_1,\dots,j_{\ell-1}}\ket{\bot}\ket{\bot}^{\otimes(d-\ell)} \mapsto \begin{cases}
            \ket{j_1,\dots,j_{\ell-1}}\ket{\bot}\ket{\bot}^{\otimes(d-\ell)}, & \text{if } u \text{ is the root of a tree decomposition}, \\
            \ket{j_1, \dots, j_{\ell-1}}\ket{\psi_u}\ket{\bot}^{\otimes(d-\ell)}, & \text{otherwise}.
        \end{cases}\]

        Then, we can implement the reflection through $\mathcal{C}_{G,r}$ in the circuit model with two calls to all the $\mathcal{E}_{\ell}$'s and $U_{\ell}$'s, and $\widetilde{O}(d\log(K))$ auxiliary elementary gates.
statement_text: Let G = (V,E) be a graph with resistances r : E → R _ >0 , and let T be a tree-parallel decomposition of the circulation space of G , with depth d . For every ell ∈ [d] , let k_ ell be the maximum number of children of nodes in the (ell -1) th vertex layer. We use a Hilbert space C ^ [k_1] ∪ {bot } ⊗ ... ⊗ C ^ [k_d] ∪ {bot } , with dimension K = (k_1+1) ... (k_d+1) . Every node u in T is connected to its root by a unique path. If u is in the ell th vertex layer, we write u = (j_1, ... , j_ell ) , if u is reached through starting at the root node and taking the j_ ell ' th child at the (ell '-1) th vertex layer, for all ell ' ∈ [ell ] . Moreover, since every leaf u = (j_1, ... , j_d) is uniquely labeled by a singleton {e} , we identify \[ |e rangle := |j_1, ... , j_d rangle .\] Next, let an internal node u ∈ V be labeled by E_u , and let u_1, ... , u_k be its children, labeled by E_ u_1 , ... , E_ u_k . Suppose that G|_ E_ u_1 , ... , G|_ E_ u_k is a parallel decomposition of G|_ E_u , with source and sink nodes s and t . For all j ∈ [k] , we write \[ |ψ_u rangle := Σ _ j=1 ^k frac 1 | |f_ u,j rangle | |j rangle , qquad with qquad |f_ u,j rangle := |f^ min _ G|_ E_ u_j , s, t, r|_ E_ u_j rangle .\] Now, for every ell ∈ [d] , we write the operation E _ ell that for all u = (j_1, ... , j_ ell -1 ) in the (ell -1) th layer of T acts for all j ∈ [k] , \[ E _ ell : |j_1, ... ,j_ ell -1 rangle |j rangle |bot rangle ^ ⊗ (d-ell ) mapsto |j_1, ... ,j_ ell -1 rangle |j rangle |bot rangle ^ ⊗ (d-ell ) , & if u is the root of a tree decomposition , |j_1, ... ,j_ ell -1 rangle |j rangle frac |f_ u,j rangle | |f_ u,j rangle | , & otherwise . \] Similarly, for all ell ∈ [d] , we write U_ ell as the operation that for all u = (j_1, ... , j_ ell -1 ) in the (ell -1) th layer of T acts as \[U_ ell : |j_1, ... ,j_ ell -1 rangle |bot rangle |bot rangle ^ ⊗ (d-ell ) mapsto |j_1, ... ,j_ ell -1 rangle |bot rangle |bot rangle ^ ⊗ (d-ell ) , & if u is the root of a tree decomposition , |j_1, ... , j_ ell -1 rangle |ψ_u rangle |bot rangle ^ ⊗ (d-ell ) , & otherwise . \] Then, we can implement the reflection through C _ G,r in the circuit model with two calls to all the E _ ell 's and U_ ell 's, and widetilde O (d log (K)) auxiliary elementary gates.

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
Let $G = (V,E)$ be an undirected multigraph with resistances $r : E \to \R_{>0}$, and $s,t \in V$ with $s \neq t$. Let $\D \subseteq \{0,1\}^n$ and for all $e \in E$, let $j(e) \in [n]$ and $b(e) \in \{0,1\}$. We refer to $\mathcal{G} = (G,j,b,r)$ as an $st$-connectivity graph on $\D$, and we say that it computes the function $f : \D \to \{0,1\}$, where $f(x) = 1$ if and only if $s$ and $t$ are connected along the graph $G(x) = (V,E(x))$, where $E(x) = \{e \in E : x_{j(e)} = b(e)\}$. We let $w_+(x,\mathcal{G}) = R_{G(x),s,t,r}$, and $w_-(x,\mathcal{G}) = R_{G,s,t,r'}^{-1}$, where $r'(e) = r(e)^{-1}$ if $x_{j(e)} \neq b(e)$, and $0$ otherwise. We say that the complexity of $\mathcal{G}$ is
        \[C(\mathcal{G}) = \sqrt{\max_{x \in f^{-1}(1)} w_+(x,\mathcal{G}) \cdot \max_{x \in f^{-1}(0)} w_-(x,\mathcal{G})}.\]
        Finally, for any boolean function $f : \D \to \{0,1\}$ with $\D \subseteq \{0,1\}^n$, we write $\st(f)$ for the minimal complexity $C(\mathcal{G})$ of an $st$-connectivity graph $\mathcal{G}$ that computes $f$.
statement_text: Let G = (V,E) be an undirected multigraph with resistances r : E → R _ >0 , and s,t ∈ V with s ≠ t . Let D ⊆ {0,1}^n and for all e ∈ E , let j(e) ∈ [n] and b(e) ∈ {0,1} . We refer to G = (G,j,b,r) as an st -connectivity graph on D , and we say that it computes the function f : D → {0,1} , where f(x) = 1 if and only if s and t are connected along the graph G(x) = (V,E(x)) , where E(x) = {e ∈ E : x_ j(e) = b(e)} . We let w_+(x, G ) = R_ G(x),s,t,r , and w_-(x, G ) = R_ G,s,t,r' ^ -1 , where r'(e) = r(e)^ -1 if x_ j(e) ≠ b(e) , and 0 otherwise. We say that the complexity of G is \[C( G ) = sqrt max _ x ∈ f^ -1 (1) w_+(x, G ) · max _ x ∈ f^ -1 (0) w_-(x, G ) .\] Finally, for any boolean function f : D → {0,1} with D ⊆ {0,1}^n , we write st (f) for the minimal complexity C( G ) of an st -connectivity graph G that computes f .

label: thm:st-connectivity
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{thm:st-connectivity}
        Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\D \subseteq \{0,1\}^n$. Every $st$-connectivity graph $\mathcal{G} = (G,j,e,r)$ on $\D$ can be turned into a graph composition $\mathcal{P}$ on $\D$, such that $C(\mathcal{P}) = C(\mathcal{G})$.
statement_text: Let n ∈ N and D ⊆ {0,1}^n . Every st -connectivity graph G = (G,j,e,r) on D can be turned into a graph composition P on D , such that C( P ) = C( G ) .

label: lem:planar-dual-circulation-space
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_text: Let G = (V,E) be a connected, undirected, planar graph, where every edge e ∈ E has an implicit direction meaning that it goes from e_- to e_+ . Let G^ dagger = (F^ dagger ,E^ dagger ) be a planar dual of G , where every edge e is associated to a dual edge e^ dagger ∈ E^ dagger , that points from the face on the left of e to the face on the right of e , as seen from the perspective of traversing e in its implicit direction. Moreover, let r : E → [0, ∞ ] be resistances on G , and let r^ dagger : E^ dagger → [0, ∞ ] be defined by r^ dagger _ e^ dagger = 1/r_e . Then, by identifying |e^ dagger rangle = |e rangle , and as such identifying H _ G^ dagger = H _G , we find that \[ H _G = C _ G,r ⊕ C _ G^ dagger ,r^ dagger = H _ G^ dagger .\]

label: thm:dual-graph-composition
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{thm:dual-graph-composition}
        Let $G = (V,E)$ be a connected, undirected graph with $s,t \in V$ and $s \neq t$, such that $G \cup \{(s,t)\}$ is planar. Let $G^{\dagger} = (F^{\dagger},E^{\dagger})$ be a planar dual of $G \cup \{(s,t)\}$ with the dual edge of $(s,t)$, connecting $s^{\dagger}$ and $t^{\dagger}$, removed. For all $e \in E$ we denote its dual edge by $e^{\dagger}$, we let $\mathcal{P}$ be the span program formed by taking the graph composition of $G$ with the span programs $(\mathcal{P}_e)_{e \in E}$, and we let $\mathcal{P}^{\dagger}$ be the graph composition of $G^{\dagger}$ with span programs $(\lnot\mathcal{P}_e)_{e^{\dagger} \in E^{\dagger}}$. Then, $\lnot\mathcal{P} = \mathcal{P}^{\dagger}$.
statement_text: Let G = (V,E) be a connected, undirected graph with s,t ∈ V and s ≠ t , such that G ∪ {(s,t)} is planar. Let G^ dagger = (F^ dagger ,E^ dagger ) be a planar dual of G ∪ {(s,t)} with the dual edge of (s,t) , connecting s^ dagger and t^ dagger , removed. For all e ∈ E we denote its dual edge by e^ dagger , we let P be the span program formed by taking the graph composition of G with the span programs ( P _e)_ e ∈ E , and we let P ^ dagger be the graph composition of G^ dagger with span programs ( ¬ P _e)_ e^ dagger ∈ E^ dagger . Then, ¬ P = P ^ dagger .

label: def:logical-compositions
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_text: Let n ∈ N , and P _1, ... , P _n be span programs on D . We define two special types of graph compositions: Let G be a line graph with n edges, and let s and t be the endpoints. We let P be the graph composition of G with span programs P _1, ... , P _n on the edges, and we write P = wedge_ j=1 ^n P _j . We refer to this as the AND-composition of P _1, ... , P _n . Let G be a graph with 2 nodes, s and t , and n parallel edges between them. We let P be the graph composition with span programs P _1, ... , P _n on the edges, and we write P = vee_ j=1 ^n P _j . We refer to this construction as the OR-composition of P _1, ... , P _n .
title: AND- and OR-composition

label: thm:and-or-witness-sizes
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{thm:and-or-witness-sizes}
        Let $\mathcal{P}_1, \dots, \mathcal{P}_n$ be span programs on a common domain $\D$. Then, for all $x \in \D$, we have
        \[w_+\left(x,\bigwedge_{j=1}^n \mathcal{P}_j\right) = \sum_{j=1}^n w_+(x,\mathcal{P}_j), \qquad \text{and} \qquad w_-\left(x,\bigwedge_{j=1}^n \mathcal{P}_j\right) = \left[\sum_{j=1}^n \frac{1}{w_-(x,\mathcal{P}_j)}\right]^{-1},\]
        and
        \[w_+\left(x,\bigvee_{j=1}^n \mathcal{P}_j\right) = \left[\sum_{j=1}^n \frac{1}{w_+(x,\mathcal{P}_j)}\right]^{-1}, \qquad \text{and} \qquad w_-\left(x,\bigvee_{j=1}^n \mathcal{P}_j\right) = \sum_{j=1}^n w_-(x,\mathcal{P}_j).\]
statement_text: Let P _1, ... , P _n be span programs on a common domain D . Then, for all x ∈ D , we have \[w_+ (x, wedge_ j=1 ^n P _j ) = Σ _ j=1 ^n w_+(x, P _j), qquad and qquad w_- (x, wedge_ j=1 ^n P _j ) = [ Σ _ j=1 ^n frac 1 w_-(x, P _j) ]^ -1 ,\] and \[w_+ (x, vee_ j=1 ^n P _j ) = [ Σ _ j=1 ^n frac 1 w_+(x, P _j) ]^ -1 , qquad and qquad w_- (x, vee_ j=1 ^n P _j ) = Σ _ j=1 ^n w_-(x, P _j).\]
title: Witness sizes of AND- and OR-composition

statement_tex:
Let $\mathcal{P}_1, \dots, \mathcal{P}_n$ be span programs on a common domain $\D$. Then,
        \[\mathcal{P} = \bigvee_{j=1}^n \frac{\mathcal{P}_j}{W_+(\mathcal{P}_j)} \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad C\left(\mathcal{P}\right)^2 \leq \sum_{j=1}^n C(\mathcal{P}_j)^2.\]
statement_text: Let P _1, ... , P _n be span programs on a common domain D . Then, \[ P = vee_ j=1 ^n frac P _j W_+( P _j) qquad ⇒ qquad C ( P )^2 ≤ Σ _ j=1 ^n C( P _j)^2.\]
title: Variable-time search

label: thm:variable-time-formula-evaluation
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{thm:variable-time-formula-evaluation}
        Let $n \in \N$, $\D \subseteq \{0,1\}^n$, and $\varphi : \D \to \{0,1\}$ be a boolean formula. Let $J(\varphi)$ be the multiset of the indices being queried by $\varphi$, e.g., $J((x_{j_1} \land x_{j_2}) \lor (\lnot x_{j_1} \land \lnot x_{j_2})) = \{j_1,j_2,j_1,j_2\}$. Let $\mathcal{P}_1, \dots, \mathcal{P}_n$ be span programs on $\D$, such that $\mathcal{P}_j$ computes the $j$th bit of $x \in \D$. Then we can build a graph composition $\mathcal{P}$ on $\D$ of a series-parallel graph $G$ that computes $\varphi$ with complexity
        \[C(\mathcal{P})^2 \leq \sum_{j \in J(\varphi)} C(\mathcal{P}_j)^2.\]
        Moreover, in the QROM-model, we can implement the reflection through the circulation space using a QROM with $\widetilde{O}(|J(\varphi)|^{d+1})$ bits, and with $\widetilde{O}\left(d^2\log|J(\varphi)|\right)$ elementary gates, where $d$ is the depth of the AND-OR-tree representation of $\varphi$.
statement_text: Let n ∈ N , D ⊆ {0,1}^n , and φ : D → {0,1} be a boolean formula. Let J(φ) be the multiset of the indices being queried by φ , e.g., J((x_ j_1 ∧ x_ j_2 ) ∨ ( ¬ x_ j_1 ∧ ¬ x_ j_2 )) = {j_1,j_2,j_1,j_2} . Let P _1, ... , P _n be span programs on D , such that P _j computes the j th bit of x ∈ D . Then we can build a graph composition P on D of a series-parallel graph G that computes φ with complexity \[C( P )^2 ≤ Σ _ j ∈ J(φ) C( P _j)^2.\] Moreover, in the QROM-model, we can implement the reflection through the circulation space using a QROM with widetilde O (|J(φ)|^ d+1 ) bits, and with widetilde O (d^2 log |J(φ)| ) elementary gates, where d is the depth of the AND-OR-tree representation of φ .
title: Variable-time formula evaluation

label: def:divide-and-conquer
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{def:divide-and-conquer}
        Let $a,b,n \in \N$, $\Sigma$ a finite alphabet, and $\Lambda$ a finite parameter space. For all $m \in \N$ and $\lambda \in \Lambda$, let $f_m^{\lambda} : \Sigma^n \to \{0,1\}$, $f_m^{\lambda,\aux} : \Sigma^n \to \{0,1\}$, $m_1, \dots, m_a \in \Theta(m/b)$, $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_a \in \Lambda$, and $\varphi_m^{\lambda} : \{0,1\}^{a+1} \to \{0,1\}$ be a boolean read-once formula, i.e., where each variable appears exactly once, such that there exists a $m_0 \in \N$, such that for all $m \geq m_0$ and $x \in \Sigma^n$,
        \[f_m^{\lambda}(x) = \varphi_m^{\lambda}(f_{m_1}^{\lambda_1}(x), \dots, f_{m_a}^{\lambda_a}(x), f_m^{\lambda,\aux}(x)).\]
        This defines a \textit{quantum divide and conquer strategy for $\{f_m^{\lambda}\}_{m \in \N, \lambda \in \Lambda}$}.
statement_text: Let a,b,n ∈ N , Σ a finite alphabet, and Λ a finite parameter space. For all m ∈ N and λ ∈ Λ , let f_m^ λ : Σ^n → {0,1} , f_m^ λ, aux : Σ^n → {0,1} , m_1, ... , m_a ∈ Θ(m/b) , λ_1, ... , λ_a ∈ Λ , and φ_m^ λ : {0,1}^ a+1 → {0,1} be a boolean read-once formula, i.e., where each variable appears exactly once, such that there exists a m_0 ∈ N , such that for all m ≥ m_0 and x ∈ Σ^n , \[f_m^ λ (x) = φ_m^ λ (f_ m_1 ^ λ_1 (x), ... , f_ m_a ^ λ_a (x), f_m^ λ, aux (x)).\] This defines a it quantum divide and conquer strategy for {f_m^ λ }_ m ∈ N , λ ∈ Λ .
title: Quantum divide and conquer,

label: thm:divide-and-conquer
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{thm:divide-and-conquer}
        Consider a quantum divide and conquer strategy for a family of functions $\{f_m^{\lambda}\}_{m \in \N, \lambda \in \Lambda}$, in the sense of \cref{def:divide-and-conquer}. For all $m \in \N$, let $\mathcal{P}_m^{\lambda,\aux}$ be a span program that evaluates $f_m^{\lambda,\aux}$, and for all $m < m_0$, let $\mathcal{P}_m^{\lambda}$ be a span program evaluating $f_m^{\lambda}$. Now, we can build a family of graph compositions $(\mathcal{P}_m^{\lambda})_{m \in \N, \lambda \in \Lambda}$, where for all $m \geq m_0$, $\mathcal{P}_m^{\lambda}$ evaluates $f_m^{\lambda}$, and satisfies
        \[C(\mathcal{P}_m^{\lambda})^2 \leq \sum_{j=1}^a C(\mathcal{P}_{m_j}^{\lambda_j})^2 + C(\mathcal{P}_m^{\lambda,\aux})^2.\]
        Moreover, in the QROM-model, the complexity of implementing the reflection through the circulation space, in the graph composition for $\mathcal{P}_m^{\lambda}$, can be done with a QROM of size $\widetilde{O}(\mathrm{poly}(a^{\log(m)/\log(b)}))$ and using $\widetilde{O}((\log(m)/\log(b))^2\log(a))$ elementary gates.
statement_text: Consider a quantum divide and conquer strategy for a family of functions {f_m^ λ }_ m ∈ N , λ ∈ Λ , in the sense of cref def:divide-and-conquer . For all m ∈ N , let P _m^ λ, aux be a span program that evaluates f_m^ λ, aux , and for all m < m_0 , let P _m^ λ be a span program evaluating f_m^ λ . Now, we can build a family of graph compositions ( P _m^ λ )_ m ∈ N , λ ∈ Λ , where for all m ≥ m_0 , P _m^ λ evaluates f_m^ λ , and satisfies \[C( P _m^ λ )^2 ≤ Σ _ j=1 ^a C( P _ m_j ^ λ_j )^2 + C( P _m^ λ, aux )^2.\] Moreover, in the QROM-model, the complexity of implementing the reflection through the circulation space, in the graph composition for P _m^ λ , can be done with a QROM of size widetilde O ( poly (a^ log (m)/ log (b) )) and using widetilde O (( log (m)/ log (b))^2 log (a)) elementary gates.

label: thm:savitch

statement_tex:
\label{thm:savitch}
        There is an $st$-connectivity algorithm that solves the directed $st$-connectivity problem making $O(\sqrt{2n}^{\log(n)})$ queries, with $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{2n}^{\log(n)})$ elementary gates, and using $O(\log^2(n))$ space.
statement_text: There is an st -connectivity algorithm that solves the directed st -connectivity problem making O( sqrt 2n ^ log (n) ) queries, with widetilde O ( sqrt 2n ^ log (n) ) elementary gates, and using O( log ^2(n)) space.

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
Let $n \in \N$, $\D \subseteq \{0,1\}^n$, and $f : \D \to \{0,1\}$. We need the following ingredients:
        \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
            \item A directed acyclic graph $G = (V,E)$.
            \item Labels $S : V \to 2^{[n]}$, such that:
            \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
                \item There is a unique $r(G) \in V$ with $S(r(G)) = \varnothing$.
                \item For all $(u,v) = e \in E$, there exists a $j \in [n]$ such that $j \not\in S(u)$ and $S(v) = S(u) \cup \{j\}$.
            \end{enumerate}
            \item A weight function $w : \D \times E \times \{0,1\} \to \R_{\geq 0}$, such that for all $(u,v) = e \in E$, $j \in [n]$ such that $S(v) = S(u) \cup \{j\}$ and $b \in \{0,1\}$:
            \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
                \item For all $x,y \in \D$, we have $x_{S(v)} = y_{S(v)}$ implies $w(x,e,b) = w(y,e,b)$.
                \item For all $(x,y) \in f^{-1}(1) \times f^{-1}(0)$, $x_{S(u)} = y_{S(u)}$ and $x_j \neq y_j$ implies $w(x,e,0) = w(y,e,1)$.
            \end{enumerate}
            \item Finally, for all $y \in f^{-1}(1)$, let $p_y : E \to \R_{\geq 0}$ be a unit flow on $G$, with:
            \begin{enumerate}[nosep]
                \item A single source node $r(G)$.
                \item The sink nodes are all the nodes $v \in V$ for which $S(v)$ contains a $1$-certificate for $y$.
                \item for all $e \in E$, $w(y,e,1) = 0$ implies $p_y(e) = 0$.
            \end{enumerate}
        \end{enumerate}
        Then $L = (G,S,w,\{p_y\}_{y \in f^{-1}(1)})$ is an \textit{adaptive learning graph} that computes $f$. For all $x \in f^{-1}(0)$ and $y \in f^{-1}(1)$, respectively, we define
        \[\ell_-(x,L) = \sum_{e \in E} w(x,e,0), \qquad \text{and} \qquad \ell_+(x,L) = \sum_{e \in E} \frac{p_y(e)^2}{w(y,e,1)},\]
        and we define
        \[\mathcal{L}_-(L) = \max_{x \in f^{-1}(0)} \ell_-(x,L), \qquad \mathcal{L}_+(L) = \max_{x \in f^{-1}(1)} \ell_+(x,L), \qquad \text{and} \qquad \mathcal{L}(L) = \sqrt{\mathcal{L}_-(L) \cdot \mathcal{L}_+(L)}.\]
        Finally, we write $\mathsf{XLG}(f)$ as the minimum of $\mathcal{L}(L)$ over all adaptive learning graphs $L$ that compute $f$.
statement_text: Let n ∈ N , D ⊆ {0,1}^n , and f : D → {0,1} . We need the following ingredients: A directed acyclic graph G = (V,E) . Labels S : V → 2^ [n] , such that: There is a unique r(G) ∈ V with S(r(G)) = varnothing . For all (u,v) = e ∈ E , there exists a j ∈ [n] such that j ∉ S(u) and S(v) = S(u) ∪ {j} . A weight function w : D × E × {0,1} → R _ ≥ 0 , such that for all (u,v) = e ∈ E , j ∈ [n] such that S(v) = S(u) ∪ {j} and b ∈ {0,1} : For all x,y ∈ D , we have x_ S(v) = y_ S(v) implies w(x,e,b) = w(y,e,b) . For all (x,y) ∈ f^ -1 (1) × f^ -1 (0) , x_ S(u) = y_ S(u) and x_j ≠ y_j implies w(x,e,0) = w(y,e,1) . Finally, for all y ∈ f^ -1 (1) , let p_y : E → R _ ≥ 0 be a unit flow on G , with: A single source node r(G) . The sink nodes are all the nodes v ∈ V for which S(v) contains a 1 -certificate for y . for all e ∈ E , w(y,e,1) = 0 implies p_y(e) = 0 . Then L = (G,S,w,{p_y}_ y ∈ f^ -1 (1) ) is an it adaptive learning graph that computes f . For all x ∈ f^ -1 (0) and y ∈ f^ -1 (1) , respectively, we define \[ell _-(x,L) = Σ _ e ∈ E w(x,e,0), qquad and qquad ell _+(x,L) = Σ _ e ∈ E frac p_y(e)^2 w(y,e,1) ,\] and we define \[ L _-(L) = max _ x ∈ f^ -1 (0) ell _-(x,L), qquad L _+(L) = max _ x ∈ f^ -1 (1) ell _+(x,L), qquad and qquad L (L) = sqrt L _-(L) · L _+(L) .\] Finally, we write XLG (f) as the minimum of L (L) over all adaptive learning graphs L that compute f .
title: Extended learning graphs

label: thm:extended-learning-graphs
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{thm:extended-learning-graphs}
        Let $L$ be an extended learning graph. Then, we can construct an instance of the $st$-connectivity framework that evaluates the learning graph, with complexity at most $\mathcal{L}(L)$. As such, for all $f : \{0,1\}^n \supseteq \D \to \{0,1\}$, $\st(f) \leq \mathcal{L}(f)$.
statement_text: Let L be an extended learning graph. Then, we can construct an instance of the st -connectivity framework that evaluates the learning graph, with complexity at most L (L) . As such, for all f : {0,1}^n ⊇ D → {0,1} , st (f) ≤ L (f) .

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
Let $n \in \N$, $\D \subseteq \{0,1\}^n$ and $f : \D \to \{0,1\}$. Let $T = (V,E)$ be a decision tree computing $f$, and let $G : E \to \{0,1\}$ be a guessing algorithm, such that for every internal node $v \in V$, exactly one of its children is connected with an edge $e \in E$ for which $G(e) = 1$. Then, we write $\mathsf{T}(T)$ for the depth of $T$, and the $\mathsf{G}(T)$ for the maximum number of edges $e \in E$ along a path from the root to a leaf that satisfy $G(e) = 0$. We call $\mathsf{G}(T)$ the guessing complexity of $T$. Finally, we write
        \[\sqrt{\mathsf{GT}}(f) = \min_{T \text{ computing } f} \sqrt{\mathsf{G}(T) \cdot \mathsf{T}(T)}.\]
statement_text: Let n ∈ N , D ⊆ {0,1}^n and f : D → {0,1} . Let T = (V,E) be a decision tree computing f , and let G : E → {0,1} be a guessing algorithm, such that for every internal node v ∈ V , exactly one of its children is connected with an edge e ∈ E for which G(e) = 1 . Then, we write T (T) for the depth of T , and the G (T) for the maximum number of edges e ∈ E along a path from the root to a leaf that satisfy G(e) = 0 . We call G (T) the guessing complexity of T . Finally, we write \[ sqrt GT (f) = min _ T computing f sqrt G (T) · T (T) .\]
title: Decision tree + guessing algorithm complexity

label: def:weighted-decision-tree
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{def:weighted-decision-tree}
        Let $n \in \N$, $\D \subseteq \{0,1\}^n$ and $f : \D \to \{0,1\}$. Let $\T = (V,E)$ be a decision tree computing $f$, and $w : E \to \R_{\geq 0}$ a weight functions on the edges. For every input $x \in \D$, let $\mathcal{P}_x$ be the path taken on input $x$, and let $\overline{\mathcal{P}}_x$ be the set of edges that have exactly one node in common with the vertices traversed in $\mathcal{P}_x$. Then, we define
        \[\WDT_+(\T,w) = \max_{x \in f^{-1}(1)} \sum_{e \in \mathcal{P}_x} w_e, \qquad \WDT_-(\T,w) = \max_{x \in f^{-1}(0)} \sum_{e \in \overline{\mathcal{P}}_x} \frac{1}{w_e},\]
        and $\WDT(\T,w) = \sqrt{\WDT_+(\T,w) \cdot \WDT_-(\T,w)}$. Moreover, we let
        \[\WDT(\T) = \min_{w : E \to \R_{\geq0}} \WDT(\T,w), \qquad \text{and} \qquad \WDT(f) = \min_{\T \text{ computing } f} \WDT(\T).\]
statement_text: Let n ∈ N , D ⊆ {0,1}^n and f : D → {0,1} . Let T = (V,E) be a decision tree computing f , and w : E → R _ ≥ 0 a weight functions on the edges. For every input x ∈ D , let P _x be the path taken on input x , and let overline P _x be the set of edges that have exactly one node in common with the vertices traversed in P _x . Then, we define \[ WDT _+( T ,w) = max _ x ∈ f^ -1 (1) Σ _ e ∈ P _x w_e, qquad WDT _-( T ,w) = max _ x ∈ f^ -1 (0) Σ _ e ∈ overline P _x frac 1 w_e ,\] and WDT ( T ,w) = sqrt WDT _+( T ,w) · WDT _-( T ,w) . Moreover, we let \[ WDT ( T ) = min _ w : E → R _ ≥ 0 WDT ( T ,w), qquad and qquad WDT (f) = min _ T computing f WDT ( T ).\]
title: Weighted-decision-tree complexity

label: def:zero-error
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{def:zero-error}
        Let $n \in \N$, $\D \subseteq \{0,1\}^n$, and $f : \D \to \{0,1\}$. Let $\mathcal{T} = \{T_1, \dots, T_k\}$ be a set of decision trees, where every leaf is labeled with $0$, $1$, or \texttt{?}. Let $ p= (p_1, \dots, p_k)$ be a probability distribution on $[k]$, such that for all $x \in \D$, if we sample $T_j$ with $j \sim p$, then the probability that it outputs $\lnot f(x)$ is $0$, and the probability that it outputs \texttt{?} is at most $1/2$. Then, we say that $\mathcal{T}$ computes $f$ with zero error, and we write
        \[\sqrt{\mathsf{GT}}(\mathcal{T}) = \max_{j \in [k]} \sqrt{\mathsf{G}(T_j) \cdot \mathsf{T}(T_j)}, \qquad \text{and} \qquad \sqrt{\mathsf{GT}}_0(f) = \min_{\mathcal{T} \text{ computes } f \text{ with zero error}} \sqrt{\mathsf{GT}}(\mathcal{T}).\]
        and
        \[\WDT(\mathcal{T}) = \max_{j \in [k]} \WDT(T_j), \qquad \text{and} \qquad \WDT_0(f) = \min_{\mathcal{T} \text{ computes } f \text{ with zero error}} \WDT(\mathcal{T}).\]
statement_text: Let n ∈ N , D ⊆ {0,1}^n , and f : D → {0,1} . Let T = {T_1, ... , T_k} be a set of decision trees, where every leaf is labeled with 0 , 1 , or tt ? . Let p= (p_1, ... , p_k) be a probability distribution on [k] , such that for all x ∈ D , if we sample T_j with j p , then the probability that it outputs ¬ f(x) is 0 , and the probability that it outputs tt ? is at most 1/2 . Then, we say that T computes f with zero error, and we write \[ sqrt GT ( T ) = max _ j ∈ [k] sqrt G (T_j) · T (T_j) , qquad and qquad sqrt GT _0(f) = min _ T computes f with zero error sqrt GT ( T ).\] and \[ WDT ( T ) = max _ j ∈ [k] WDT (T_j), qquad and qquad WDT _0(f) = min _ T computes f with zero error WDT ( T ).\]
title: Zero-error version of the complexity measures

label: thm:weighted-decision-trees
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{thm:weighted-decision-trees}
        Let $\T = (V,E)$ be a decision tree, making queries to an $n$-bit string, having outputs in $\{0,1,\texttt{?}\}$, and with a weight function $w : E \to \R_{>0}$ on the edges. Then, we can construct an instance of the $st$-connectivity framework that distinguishes whether the output of the tree is $1$ or an element of $\{0,\texttt{?}\}$ with complexity at most $\WDT(\T,w)$.
statement_text: Let T = (V,E) be a decision tree, making queries to an n -bit string, having outputs in {0,1,tt ? } , and with a weight function w : E → R _ >0 on the edges. Then, we can construct an instance of the st -connectivity framework that distinguishes whether the output of the tree is 1 or an element of {0,tt ? } with complexity at most WDT ( T ,w) .

label: thm:threshold
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{thm:threshold}
        Let $n \in \N$, and $k \in \{1, \dots, n\}$. Let $f_n^k$ be the threshold function on $n$ bits with threshold $k$, i.e., $f_n^k(x) = 1$ if and only if $|x| \geq k$. Let $x_j$ be a trivial span program computing the $j$th bit of the input. Then, for all $\S \subseteq [n]$, we recursively define
        \[\Th_\S^{k+1} = \bigvee_{j \in \S} (x_j \land k\Th_{\S \setminus \{j\}}^k), \qquad \text{and} \qquad \Th_\S^1 = \bigvee_{j \in \S} x_j.\]
        Then, $\Th_n^k := \Th_{[n]}^k$ computes $f_n^k$, with witness sizes
        \[w_+(x,\Th_n^k) = \begin{cases}
            \frac{1}{|x|-k+1}, & \text{if } |x| \geq k, \\
            \infty, & \text{otherwise},
        \end{cases} \qquad \text{and} \qquad w_-(x,\Th_n^k) = \begin{cases}
            \infty, & \text{if } |x| \geq k, \\
            \frac{k(n-k+1)}{k-|x|}, & \text{otherwise}.
        \end{cases}\]
        Consequently, $C(\Th_n^k) = \sqrt{k(n+k-1)}$, and this is optimal.
statement_text: Let n ∈ N , and k ∈ {1, ... , n} . Let f_n^k be the threshold function on n bits with threshold k , i.e., f_n^k(x) = 1 if and only if |x| ≥ k . Let x_j be a trivial span program computing the j th bit of the input. Then, for all S ⊆ [n] , we recursively define \[ Th _ S ^ k+1 = vee_ j ∈ S (x_j ∧ k Th _ S \ {j} ^k), qquad and qquad Th _ S ^1 = vee_ j ∈ S x_j.\] Then, Th _n^k := Th _ [n] ^k computes f_n^k , with witness sizes \[w_+(x, Th _n^k) = frac 1 |x|-k+1 , & if |x| ≥ k, ∞ , & otherwise , qquad and qquad w_-(x, Th _n^k) = ∞ , & if |x| ≥ k, frac k(n-k+1) k-|x| , & otherwise . \] Consequently, C( Th _n^k) = sqrt k(n+k-1) , and this is optimal.
title: Threshold functions through the st -connectivity framework

label: thm:exact-weight
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{thm:exact-weight}
        Let $n \in \N$, $k \in \{1, \dots, n-1\}$, and let $f_n^k$ be the exact-weight function on $n$ bits with weight $k$, i.e., $f_n^k(x) = 1$ if and only if $|x| = k$. We let
        \[\EW_n^k = k(n+k-1)\Th_n^k \land \lnot \Th_n^{k+1}.\]
        Then, $\EW_n^k$ computes $f_n^k$, with witness sizes
        \[w_+(x,\EW_n^k) = \begin{cases}
            n + 2k(n-k), & \text{if } |x| = k, \\
            \infty, & \text{otherwise},
        \end{cases} \qquad \text{and} \qquad w_-(x,\EW_n^k) = \begin{cases}
            \infty, & \text{if } |x| = k, \\
            \frac{1}{|k-|x||}, & \text{otherwise}.
        \end{cases}\]
        Consequently, $C(\EW_n^k) = \sqrt{n + 2k(n-k)}$, and this is optimal.
statement_text: Let n ∈ N , k ∈ {1, ... , n-1} , and let f_n^k be the exact-weight function on n bits with weight k , i.e., f_n^k(x) = 1 if and only if |x| = k . We let \[ EW _n^k = k(n+k-1) Th _n^k ∧ ¬ Th _n^ k+1 .\] Then, EW _n^k computes f_n^k , with witness sizes \[w_+(x, EW _n^k) = n + 2k(n-k), & if |x| = k, ∞ , & otherwise , qquad and qquad w_-(x, EW _n^k) = ∞ , & if |x| = k, frac 1 |k-|x|| , & otherwise . \] Consequently, C( EW _n^k) = sqrt n + 2k(n-k) , and this is optimal.
title: Graph-composition for the exact-weight function

label: lem:gapped-majority
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{lem:gapped-majority}
        Let $n \in \N$, $\D = \{x \in \{0,1\}^n : |x| < n/3 \lor |x| > 2n/3\}$, and $f_n : \D \to \{0,1\}$ be defined as $f_n(x) = 1$ if and only if $|x| > 2n/3$. That is, $f_n$ is the gapped majority function on $n$ inputs. Then, $\mathsf{st}(f_n) \in O(1)$, and $\mathsf{R}_0(f_n) \in \Omega(n)$.
statement_text: Let n ∈ N , D = {x ∈ {0,1}^n : |x| < n/3 ∨ |x| > 2n/3} , and f_n : D → {0,1} be defined as f_n(x) = 1 if and only if |x| > 2n/3 . That is, f_n is the gapped majority function on n inputs. Then, st (f_n) ∈ O(1) , and R _0(f_n) ∈ Ω(n) .

label: thm:GT-sep-WDT
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{thm:GT-sep-WDT}
        Let $n \in \N$ and $f : \{0,1\}^{2n+1} \to \{0,1\}$ be defined as
        \[f(x) = \begin{cases}
            x_2 \oplus x_3 \oplus \cdots \oplus x_{n+1}, & \text{if } x_1 = 1, \\
            x_2 \lor x_3 \lor \cdots \lor x_{n^2+1}, & \text{if } x_1 = 0.
        \end{cases}.\]
        Then, $\WDT(f) \in O(n)$ and $\sqrt{\GT}_0(f) \in \Omega(n^{3/2})$.
statement_text: Let n ∈ N and f : {0,1}^ 2n+1 → {0,1} be defined as \[f(x) = x_2 ⊕ x_3 ⊕ ... ⊕ x_ n+1 , & if x_1 = 1, x_2 ∨ x_3 ∨ ... ∨ x_ n^2+1 , & if x_1 = 0. .\] Then, WDT (f) ∈ O(n) and sqrt GT _0(f) ∈ Ω(n^ 3/2 ) .

label: lem:deterministic-sample
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{lem:deterministic-sample}
        Let $\Sigma$ a finite alphabet of constant size, $m,n \in \N$ and $y \in \Sigma^m$ aperiodic, i.e., there does not exist a $p \leq m/2$ such that $y_{kp+\ell} = y_\ell$ for all $\ell \in [p]$ and $0 \leq k \leq \lfloor(n-\ell)/p\rfloor$. Then, there exists a subset $J \subseteq [m]$ and integer $0 \leq k \leq m/2$ such that $|J| \leq \log(m)$, and such that if $x[j:j+m-1]$ agrees with $y$ on $J$, with $j \in [n-m+1]$, then for any non-zero integer $\max\{0,-k\} \leq \ell \leq \min\{m/2-k,n-m+1\}$, $x[j+\ell:j+m-1+\ell]$ does not agree with $y$.
statement_text: Let Σ a finite alphabet of constant size, m,n ∈ N and y ∈ Σ^m aperiodic, i.e., there does not exist a p ≤ m/2 such that y_ kp+ell = y_ell for all ell ∈ [p] and 0 ≤ k ≤ lfloor (n-ell )/prfloor . Then, there exists a subset J ⊆ [m] and integer 0 ≤ k ≤ m/2 such that |J| ≤ log (m) , and such that if x[j:j+m-1] agrees with y on J , with j ∈ [n-m+1] , then for any non-zero integer max {0,-k} ≤ ell ≤ min {m/2-k,n-m+1} , x[j+ell :j+m-1+ell ] does not agree with y .
title: Deterministic sample

label: thm:aperiodic-pattern-matching
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{thm:aperiodic-pattern-matching}
        Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet of constant size, and $y \in \Sigma^m$ an aperiodic pattern. We can solve the aperiodic pattern matching problem with $O(\sqrt{n\log(m)})$ queries to the input string $x \in \Sigma^n$, $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$ elementary gates, and a QROM of size $O(m)$.
statement_text: Let Σ be a finite alphabet of constant size, and y ∈ Σ^m an aperiodic pattern. We can solve the aperiodic pattern matching problem with O( sqrt n log (m) ) queries to the input string x ∈ Σ^n , widetilde O ( sqrt n ) elementary gates, and a QROM of size O(m) .
title: Quantum algorithm for aperiodic pattern matching

label: thm:pattern-matching
paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
\label{thm:pattern-matching}
        Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet of constant size, $n,m \in \N$ and $y \in \Sigma^m$ be a periodic pattern with period $p$, and $k = \lceil m/p\rceil \geq 2$ (partial) repetitions. Then, we can solve the pattern matching problem with $O(\sqrt{n\log(p)})$ queries to the input string $x \in \Sigma^n$.
statement_text: Let Σ be a finite alphabet of constant size, n,m ∈ N and y ∈ Σ^m be a periodic pattern with period p , and k = lceil m/prceil ≥ 2 (partial) repetitions. Then, we can solve the pattern matching problem with O( sqrt n log (p) ) queries to the input string x ∈ Σ^n .
title: Quantum algorithm for pattern matching

paper_title: Quantum algorithms through graph composition
statement_tex:
Let $n \in \N$, and let $\D_n \subseteq \{0,1,*\}^n$, such that $x \in \D_n$ if and only if $x$ has exactly one position $j(x) \in [n]$ for which $x_{j(x)} \neq *$. The $\pSEARCH$-problem asks to output the value of $x_{j(x)}$, given query access to $x$.

        Next, let $m \in \N$, $T \in \{m,m+1,\dots,nm\}$ and let $\D_T \subseteq \D_n^m$, such that $(x^{(1)}, \dots, x^{(m)}) \in \D_T$ if and only if $j(x^{(1)}) + \cdots + j(x^{(m)}) = T$ and $|\overline{x}| \in \{0,1\}$, where
        \[\overline{x} = x^{(1)}_{j(x^{(1)})} \cdots x^{(m)}_{j(x^{(m)})} \in \{0,1\}^m.\]
        The $\OR \circ \pSEARCH$-problem asks to output $|\overline{x}|$, given query-access to $x \in \D_T$.
statement_text: Let n ∈ N , and let D _n ⊆ {0,1,*}^n , such that x ∈ D _n if and only if x has exactly one position j(x) ∈ [n] for which x_ j(x) ≠ * . The pSEARCH -problem asks to output the value of x_ j(x) , given query access to x . label: ex:incompletenessOfSymHilbert

statement_tex:
\label{ex:incompletenessOfSymHilbert}
	Let the variable set be $X = \{x_1, x_1^*, x_2, x_2^*\}$ and let $\Gamma \leq \Sym(X)$ be the group that is generated by $\{\pi,\pi^*\}$ defined as follows: $\pi = (x_1 \ x_2) \circ (x_1^* \ x_2^*)$, and $\pi^* = (x_1 \ x_1^*) \circ (x_2 \ x_2^*)$. That is, $\pi$ exchanges $1$ and $2$, and $\pi^*$ exchanges non-star with star. Consider the following equations over $\bbF_2$:\\
	\begin{tabular}{ccc}
		 (1) $x_1 + x_2 = 1$       &   (3) $x_1^*+x_2 = 1$       &  (5) $x_1 + x_1^* = 1$       \\
		  (2) $x_1^* + x_2^* = 1$ & (4) $x_1+x_2^* = 1$ & (6) $x_2 + x_2^* = 1$\\
	\end{tabular}	 
	~\\
	The equations are partitioned into three $\Gamma$-orbits. Equation (1) and (2) form an orbit, equation (3) and (4) as well, and equation (5) and (6).
	The system is unsatisfiable over $\bbF_2$ (and its algebraic closure) because $(1)+(4)+(6)$ is an IPS certificate of unsatisfiability.
	Nonetheless, there is no linear $\Gamma$-symmetric refutation $C(\vec x, \vec y)$: 
	Every monomial in such a certificate $C(\vec x, \vec y)$ would contain exactly one $\vec y$-variable. 
	In order to have $C(\vec x, \vec f) = 1$, there must be a degree-$1$ monomial in $C(\vec x, \vec y)$, i.e.\ consisting only of a single $\vec y$-variable $y_i$. But then, the entire orbit of $y_i$ must appear in $C(\vec x, \vec y)$ due to symmetry. As each orbit of equations has even size and the field has characteristic $2$, the constant terms in $C(\vec x, \vec f)$ sum up to $0$. Hence, there is no symmetric $\vec y$-linear polynomial with $C(\vec x, \vec f) = 1$.

That is, π exchanges 1 and 2 , and π^* exchanges non-star with star. Consider the following equations over bbF _2 : ccc (1) x_1 + x_2 = 1 & (3) x_1^*+x_2 = 1 & (5) x_1 + x_1^* = 1 (2) x_1^* + x_2^* = 1 & (4) x_1+x_2^* = 1 & (6) x_2 + x_2^* = 1 The equations are partitioned into three Γ -orbits. Equation (1) and (2) form an orbit, equation (3) and (4) as well, and equation (5) and (6). The system is unsatisfiable over bbF _2 (and its algebraic closure) because (1)+(4)+(6) is an IPS certificate of unsatisfiability. Nonetheless, there is no linear Γ -symmetric refutation C(vec x, vec y) : Every monomial in such a certificate C(vec x, vec y) would contain exactly one vec y -variable. label: ex:norm-wise-bad

statement_text: Let v =(10^ 15 ,1) , widetilde v =(10^ 15 (1+ε),0) , and ε=10^ -5 . Note that the second entry of v and widetilde v are very different from each other. Then frac lVert widetilde v - v rVert _1 lVert v rVert _1 = frac ε · 10^ 15 +1 10^ 15 +1 = frac 10^ 10 +1 10^ 15 +1 ≈ 10^ -5 . This means that widetilde v approximates v in a norm-wise manner, but entry-wise v and widetilde v are very different vectors. Therefore a bound on the norm does not necessarily provide bounds for the entries. For the norm bound to give guarantees for the entries, we would need to have ε ≈ frac v _ min v _ max , where v _ min and v _ max are the smallest and largest entry of v in terms of absolute value, respectively.

label: def:rddl
paper_title: Entrywise Approximation for Matrix Inversion and Linear Systems
statement_tex:
\label{def:rddl}
    A matrix $\MM\in \R^{n\times n}$ is an $L$-matrix if for all $i\neq j$, $\MM_{ij} \leq 0$, and for all $i\in [n]$, $\MM_{ii} > 0$. 
    $\MM$ is row diagonally dominant (RDD) if for all $i\in[n]$, $|\MM_{ii}| \geq \sum_{j\in [n] \setminus\{i\}} |\MM_{ij}|$. 
    $\MM$ is RDDL if it is both an $L$-matrix and RDD. 
    An SDDM matrix is an invertible \emph{symmetric} RDDL matrix.
statement_text: A matrix M ∈ R ^ n × n is an L -matrix if for all i ≠ j , M _ ij ≤ 0 , and for all i ∈ [n] , M _ ii > 0 . M is row diagonally dominant (RDD) if for all i ∈ [n] , | M _ ii | ≥ Σ _ j ∈ [n] \ {i} | M _ ij | . M is RDDL if it is both an L -matrix and RDD. An SDDM matrix is an invertible symmetric RDDL matrix.
title: RDDL and SDDM Matrices

label: def:rddl-graph
paper_title: Entrywise Approximation for Matrix Inversion and Linear Systems
statement_tex:
\label{def:rddl-graph}
    For an RDDL matrix $\MM \in \R^{n \times n}$, we define the associated weighted graph $G = ([n+1], E, w)$ with an additional dummy vertex $n+1$. 
    For any $i,j \in [n]$ with $i\neq j$, we set the edge weight $w(i,j)$ in the graph to $-\MM_{ij}$. 
    Moreover, we set the edge weight $w(i, n+1)$ to $\sum_{j \in [n]} \MM_{ij}$. 
    Finally, for all $i\in[n]$,
    if the matrix is RDDL, we set $w(n+1,i)=0$, and if the matrix is SDDM,
    we set $w(n+1,i)=w(i,n+1)$.
    
    If for all vertices $i\in[n]$, there is a path in $G$ from $i$ to $n+1$ with all positive edge weights, then we say $G$ (the graph associated to the RDDL matrix) is \emph{connected to the dummy vertex}.
statement_text: For an RDDL matrix M ∈ R ^ n × n , we define the associated weighted graph G = ([n+1], E, w) with an additional dummy vertex n+1 . For any i,j ∈ [n] with i ≠ j , we set the edge weight w(i,j) in the graph to - M _ ij . Moreover, we set the edge weight w(i, n+1) to Σ _ j ∈ [n] M _ ij . Finally, for all i ∈ [n] , if the matrix is RDDL, we set w(n+1,i)=0 , and if the matrix is SDDM, we set w(n+1,i)=w(i,n+1) . If for all vertices i ∈ [n] , there is a path in G from i to n+1 with all positive edge weights, then we say G (the graph associated to the RDDL matrix) is connected to the dummy vertex .
title: Associated Graph of an RDDL Matrix

\label{def:absorption}
Let $T$ be a subset of vertices and $s$ be a vertex. The absorption probabilities $\P_{\textrm{abs}}(s,T) \in [0,1]^{|T|}$ form a vector where the $t$-th entry denotes the probability of hitting $t \in T$ before hitting any vertex in $T \setminus \{t\}$ in all possible random walks starting at $s$. For a subset of vertices $S$, we define $\P_{\textrm{abs}}(S,T) \in [0,1]^{|S| \times |T|}$ as a matrix with $(\P_{\textrm{abs}}(S,T))_{i_s:} = (\P_{\textrm{abs}}(s,T))^\top$ for all $s \in S$, where $i_s$ is the row index associated with $s$.

For a subset of vertices S , we define P _ rm abs (S,T) ∈ [0,1]^ |S| × |T| as a matrix with ( P _ rm abs (S,T))_ i_s: = ( P _ rm abs (s,T))^top for all s ∈ S , where i_s is the row index associated with s .

label: thm:matrix-tree
paper_title: Entrywise Approximation for Matrix Inversion and Linear Systems
statement_tex:
\label{thm:matrix-tree}
Let $\MM \in \R^{n\times n}$ be an RDDL matrix such that for all $i\in [n]$, $\sum_{j\in [n]} \MM_{ij} = 0$. Let $i \in [n]$ and $\NN$ be the matrix obtained by removing row $i$ and column $i$ from $\MM$. Then $\det(\NN) = \sum_{F \in \mathcal{F}} \prod_{e\in F} w_e$, where $\mathcal{F}$ is the set of all spanning trees oriented towards vertex $i$ in the graph corresponding to matrix $\MM$. $\prod_{e\in F} w_e$ is the product of the weights of the edges of spanning tree $F$.

Then det ( N ) = Σ _ F ∈ F Π _ e ∈ F w_e , where F is the set of all spanning trees oriented towards vertex i in the graph corresponding to matrix M . Π _ e ∈ F w_e is the product of the weights of the edges of spanning tree F .

label: def:hitting-time
paper_title: Entrywise Approximation for Matrix Inversion and Linear Systems
statement_text: For a (directed or undirected and weighted or unweighted) graph G=(V,E) and s,t ∈ V , we define the hitting time of s to t , as the expected number of steps for a random walk starting from s to reach t for the first time. More formally, let W_ st ={w=(v_1, ... ,v_k): k ∈ N , ∀ i ∈ [k], ∀ j ∈ [k-1], v_i ∈ V, (v_j,v_ j+1 ) ∈ E,v_j ≠ t, v_1=s, v_k = t}, be the set of all possible walks from s to t that visit t only once. We set the probability of the random walk w=(v_1, ... ,v_k) equal to bf Pr (w):= bf Pr (v_1,v_2) bf Pr (v_2,v_3) ... bf Pr (v_ k-1 ,v_k) , where bf Pr (u,v) is the probability of going from vertex u to v in one step. We also denote the size of w with |w| which is the number of edges traversed in w , i.e., for w=(v_1, ... ,v_k) , |w|=k-1 . Then the hitting time of s to t is H(s,t):= Σ _ w ∈ W_ st bf Pr (w) · |w|. If there is no path from s to t , i.e., W_ st = ∅ , then H(s,t)= ∞ .

\label{lemma:2t}
For a (directed or undirected and weighted or unweighted) graph $G=(V,E)$ and $s,t,p\in V$, let $\overline{G} =(\overline{V},\overline{E})$ be the graph obtained by contracting (identifying) $t$ and $p$. 
Let $q$ be the vertex corresponding to $t$ and $p$ in $\overline{G}$.

Let $\AA$ be the random walk matrix associated with graph $G=(V,E)$ in which the rows corresponding to $t$ and $p$ are zeroed out.
Then for any $h$ and any $k \ge 2h$ such that
\[
h
\geq
1+\max_{s \in \overline{V}} \overline{H}\left(s,q)\right.
\]
we have

\leq
\frac{1}{2}
\qquad
\forall u \in V .

That is, any row of $\AA^{k}$ sums up to less than $0.5$, and thus $\|\AA^k\|_\infty \le 0.5.$

label: def:sum-of-squares

statement_tex:
\label{def:sum-of-squares} 
Given a set of $m$ polynomial equality constraints $\Axioms$ over the reals, a Sum of Squares (SoS) refutation is a sequence of polynomials $\Proof = (t_1, \dots, t_m; s_1, \dots, s_a)$ such that

\[ h \Def \sum_{i \in [m]} t_ip_i+ \sum_{i \in [a]} s_i^2 = -1\]

The degree of a proof $\Proof$ is

\[ \Degree{\Proof} \Def \max\left\{\max_{i \in [m]} \Degree{t_i} + \Degree{p_i}, \max_{i \in [a]} 2\Degree{s_i}\right\}\]
statement_text: Given a set of m polynomial equality constraints Q over the reals, a Sum of Squares (SoS) refutation is a sequence of polynomials π = (t_1, ... , t_m; s_1, ... , s_a) such that \[ h = Σ _ i ∈ [m] t_ip_i+ Σ _ i ∈ [a] s_i^2 = -1\] The degree of a proof π is \[ Deg (π ) = max {max _ i ∈ [m] Deg (t_i ) + Deg (p_i ), max _ i ∈ [a] 2 Deg (s_i ) }\]
title: Sum Of Squares Refutation

The degree of the proof is given by $\Degree{\Proof} = \max_{i \in l}\Degree{t_i}$. If we let $\Pi$ denote the set of all PC refutations of $\Axioms$, then

\[ \Degree{\Axioms \PC \bot} \Def \min_{\Proof \in \Pi}\Degree{\Proof}\]
statement_text: A Polynomial Calculus (PC) refutation of Q over F is a sequence of polynomials π = (t_1, ... , t_l) such that t_l = 1 , and for each i ≠ l , either (1) t_i ∈ Q , or (2) t_i is derived from {t_j}_ j < i using the above rules. The degree of the proof is given by Deg (π ) = max _ i ∈ l Deg (t_i ) . If we let Π denote the set of all PC refutations of Q , then \[ Deg ( Q vdash _ tt PC _F bot ) = min _ π ∈ Π Deg (π )\]

Let B ⊆ V(G) be a subset of size |B| ≥ n/20 , and H is any graph with maximum degree at most D and at most α frac n log n vertices. Then the induced sub-graph G[B] contains H^ σ such that σ(e) is odd for every e ∈ E(H) .

label: thm:perfect-matching
paper_title: Refuting Perfect Matchings in Spectral Expanders is Hard
statement_tex:
\label{thm:perfect-matching}
Let $G$ be an  $(n, d, \lambda)$-graph with $\lambda < d/50$, and suppose $G' \subseteq G$ satisfies $\delta(G') \ge 0.9d$. Then for all $S \subseteq V(G')$, $G' \setminus S$ has at most $|S|$ connected components, that is, $q(G' \setminus S) \le |S|$. Therefore, if $G'$ has an even number of vertices then it contains a perfect matching.
statement_text: Let G be an (n, d, λ) -graph with λ < d/50 , and suppose G' ⊆ G satisfies δ(G') ≥ 0.9d . Then for all S ⊆ V(G') , G' \ S has at most |S| connected components, that is, q(G' \ S) ≤ |S| . Therefore, if G' has an even number of vertices then it contains a perfect matching.

If $G' \subseteq G$ has minimum degree $\MinimalDegree{G'} \ge d - C$, then $G'$ contains a spanning $f$-regular subgraph for any even $2 \le f \le d/2$.

label: def:most-killing
paper_title: The Proof Analysis Problem
statement_text: We will say that a restriction ρ enjoys the most-killing property with respect to a trace τ = ((b_1, X_1), ... , (b_ell , X_ell )) if it holds that for every k ∈ [ell ] , the block i ∈ [s] \ { b_1, ... , b_ k-1 } that is the most frequent block mentioned in W_ restriction ρ_ k-1 happens to be precisely b_k and ρ_k satisfies the following conditions. sep=0pt If e_i appears positively in at least 1/3 of all the clauses in W_ restriction ρ_ k-1 that mention block i , then ρ_k(e_i) = 1 and ρ_k(x) = * for every other variable x ≠ e_i in block i . If e_i does not appear positively in at least 1/3 of all the clauses in W_ restriction ρ_ k-1 that mention block i , then ρ_k(e_i) = 0 and for every other variable in block i , ρ_k assigns values to them respecting the ordering in X_i = ( e_i, x_ i,1 , x_ i, 2 , ... ) and with the following priority. For j = 1, ... , |X_i|-1 , sep=0pt if x_ i, j appears positively more often than negatively in W_ restriction ρ_ k-1, {e_i, x_ i, 1 , ... , x_ i, j-1 } , then ρ_k(x_ i, j ) = 1 ; if x_ i, j appears negatively more often than positively in W_ restriction ρ_ k-1, {e_i, x_ i, 1 , ... , x_ i, j-1 } , then ρ_k(x_ i, j ) = 0 .
title: Most-killing property

label: lemma:induction-restriction-PV
paper_title: The Proof Analysis Problem
statement_text: Let c ∈ N . The following is provable in S^1_2 . For every CNF formula φ over n variables and π a correct Resolution refutation of normal scshape Ref _s(φ) , let w coloneq c · lceil sqrt s log |π| rceil and let W denote the set of clauses in π of block-width larger than w . Then, for every ell , the formula Ψ(φ, π, s, ell ) defined as follows holds: if ell ≤ w/2 , then there exists a restriction ρ ∈ { 0,1,*}^N , where N is the number of variables of the normal scshape Ref _s(φ) formula, a trace τ = ((b_1, X_1), ... , (b_ell , X_ell )) and d ≤ ell such that: sep=0pt ρ is d -disabling; ρ has the most-killing property according to τ ; (3s)^ell · |W_ restriction ρ | ≤ |W| · (3s- w + ell )^ell .

label: def:reservation-invariant
paper_title: The Proof Analysis Problem
statement_text: Let π be a Resolution refutation of normal scshape Ref _s(φ) for some CNF formula φ(x_1, ... , x_n) , let N be the number of variables of normal scshape Ref _s(φ) , d ≤ depth (π) , and let C = (C_1, ... , C_d) be a length- d path in π starting from C_1 = bot . Let the s blocks of normal scshape Ref _s(φ) be arranged in a layered manner, so that there are n layers, each containing lfloor s/nrfloor blocks, with the remainder blocks left from the flooring operations collected all in the last layer, plus one additional layer on top with a single block corresponding to the root. We say that C satisfies the reservation invariant with respect to a sequence A = (α_1, ... , α_d) of restrictions α_i ∈ { 0,1,*}^N if, for every i ∈ [d] , sep=0pt the restriction α_i falsifies C_i ; a block is only mentioned in α_i if it is either mentioned in C_i or its parent according to α_i is mentioned in C_i , and, in particular, bw (α_i) ≤ 3 bw (C_i) ; if α_i restricts some variable in block B from layer ell , then it does so in the following way: B must contain exactly ell literals over the variables x_1, ... , x_ell and no two literals for the same variable; the restriction α_i does not falsify any clause of normal scshape Ref _s(φ) ; the path determined by C corresponds to A in the following way: if C_i was derived from C_ i+1 by resolving over variable v , then α_ i+1 (v) is defined and v appears in C_ i+1 with polarity 1- α_ i+1 (v) .
title: Reservation invariant

label: lemma:induction-width-PV
paper_title: The Proof Analysis Problem
statement_text: The following is provable in S^1_2 . For every CNF formula φ over n variables and π a correct Resolution refutation of normal scshape Ref _s(φ) , for every d , the formula Ψ(φ, π, s, d) defined as follows holds: if 1 ≤ d ≤ depth (π) , then there exists a sequence C = (C_1, ... , C_d) of clauses of π and a sequence A = (α_1, ... , α_d) of restrictions such that at least one of the following conditions holds: sep=0pt there is C_i ∈ C that satisfies bw (C_i) ≥ 1/3 (lfloor s/n rfloor - 1 ) ; there is C_i in and its corresponding restriction α_i that contain a satisfying assignment to φ ; the sequence C is a path in π starting at C_1 = bot and the reservation invariant holds for C with respect to A .
